items.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And Elvin Jones. I just — the list is endless.

ctx.x: Do you have a list of must-listen-to drummers for young players?

Well, Mel Lewis is one of my absolute idols. I think he swings. Big band drummers I divide into two categories, Mel Lewis for sure and I love Buddy Rich, I always loved Buddy Rich. He’s like one of the, you know you can pick out the geniuses like Oscar Peterson on the piano and Buddy, like people who do, and Art Tatum, people who could play what nobody will ever be able to duplicate what these people have done, and he’s one of those. I love Jeff Hamilton right now who is a drummer in Los Angeles, one of my…
What’s the IAJE — do they have a mission to increase the audience for jazz as well as the players?

items.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: let me check out wow, all these things of Max Roach or Elvin Jones or Philly Joe Jones or any drummer

ctx.x: Well that’s one upside. I’m curious what does a drumset player practice for five hours?

Oh my gosh, well I spend a lot of time working on different, and this is recently, just different technical things and technical approaches. Like there’s a lot more than one way to hit a drum, this way, there’s using your fingers, there’s using every finger, there’s stick placement, there’s wrist movement, there’s certain bounce techniques and with both hands and both feet I just, stuff like that, I’m like wow. Like for example on thing I practice quite a bit it’s called a push/pull technique and a lot of…
Well not only that I think you just gave a brief lesson to like wind players — that was some pretty cool double tonguing you just did [scats].
